back: L4 routes by IP + port (fast, no content inspection). L7 terminates TLS, parses HTTP, and routes by URL, headers, cookies (slower but more flexible).
Requests go to backends 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3… Simple, assumes equal capacity and equal request cost.
Each backend has a weight. Higher weight = more requests. Useful when backends have different capacities.
Send to the backend with the fewest active connections. Adapts to variable request durations: slow servers get fewer requests.
Maps servers and keys to a hash ring. Each key goes to the nearest server. Adding/removing a server moves only ≈1/n of keys.
The LB periodically probes each backend (HTTP, TCP). Backends that fail multiple checks are removed from the pool.
The LB monitors real traffic. Too many 5xx errors or timeouts from a backend → mark unhealthy. Catches issues that active checks miss.
Before shutdown, the server signals unhealthy. The LB stops new traffic. In-flight requests complete. Then the server shuts down.
Uneven load (hot servers), fragile failover (session lost on crash), hard to scale (new servers only get new sessions).
Store session state externally (Redis, database, encrypted cookie). Any server can handle any request.

front: How to make the LB not a SPOF?
back: Active-passive: two LBs share a VIP; passive takes over on failure. Active-active: both handle traffic simultaneously.
A floating IP shared between redundant LBs. If the active LB fails, the passive claims the VIP. Clients see no change.

front: When to use consistent hashing in LB?
back: When backends are stateful (caches, sharded databases) and you want to minimise key redistribution on scale events.
Active-passive: one handles traffic, one is standby. Active-active: both handle traffic, doubling capacity and redundancy.
Critical dependencies: database connection, disk space, memory. Return 200 OK if healthy, 503 if not. Do not always return 200.
